title: IoT-23: A labeled dataset with malicious and benign IoT network traffic
abstract: IoT-23 is a dataset of network traffic from Internet of Things (IoT) devices. It has 20 malware captures executed in IoT devices, and 3 captures for benign IoT devices traffic. It was first published in January 2020, with captures ranging from 2018 to 2019. These IoT network traffic was captured in the Stratosphere Laboratory, AIC group, FEL, CTU University, Czech Republic. Its goal is to offer a large dataset of real and labeled IoT malware infections and IoT benign traffic for researchers to develop machine learning algorithms. This dataset and its research was funded by Avast Software. The malware was allow to connect to the Internet.

narrative:
Short impact summary

IoT-23 has become a widely used reference dataset for IoT security research, with 235 scholarly citations, 10,893 downloads, and 282 documented downstream reuses. Its impact is concentrated in network security, intrusion detection, and malware detection research, where it is repeatedly cited as a practical benchmark for work on malicious and benign IoT traffic.

Full narrative

Published in 2020 on Zenodo by Sebastián García, Agustin Parmisano, and María José Erquiaga, IoT-23 provides labeled network traffic from real IoT devices, including malware-infected and benign captures. The dataset was designed as infrastructure for the field: a reusable resource that researchers can cite, compare against, and build on when testing intrusion detection and traffic-analysis methods. The record shows sustained scholarly uptake, with citations spread across articles, conference papers, reviews, book chapters, and preprints.

The citation landscape suggests that IoT-23 has settled into the core literature of IoT and network defense. Most citing works are in network security and intrusion detection, with strong representation in advanced malware detection and anomaly detection. It is also visible in high-profile venues such as IEEE Access, Computer Networks, Sensors, Computers & Security, and ACM Computing Surveys, indicating that the dataset is not only being used, but is being used in work with broad visibility across the security community.

Usage data reinforce that pattern of reuse. The dataset has attracted substantial direct engagement in Zenodo, and the downstream reuse record shows that it is repeatedly incorporated into new studies rather than cited only as background. Crossref data-citation links and scite’s citation statements both point to active scholarly incorporation, with at least one supporting citation statement and many additional mentions in the literature. The surrounding work also spans institutions and countries across a wide international network, with education-sector users dominating the observed citing landscape.

Overall, IoT-23 functions as a foundational benchmark for IoT malware and benign traffic analysis. Its impact is best understood not as a single burst of attention, but as durable infrastructural value: a labeled dataset that researchers continue to return to when developing, evaluating, and comparing security methods for connected devices.
